title: AI Compute Goes on Credit: SpaceX Seeks $40B for Nvidia Chips as Broadcom Eyes $60B
subhead: Two giant debt packages — a $40 billion raise for SpaceX led by Apollo and a $60 billion-plus financing for Broadcom's Anthropic chips — mark a shift: frontier compute is increasingly bought with borrowed money rather than paid for out of cash flow.

sections.heading: SpaceX Taps Debt Markets for a $40 Billion Nvidia Order
sections.body:
SpaceX is seeking to raise about $40 billion to buy Nvidia AI chips, in a financing effort led by asset manager Apollo Global Management, according to an FT report carried by Reuters. The package is split between roughly $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt, with the deal potentially closing in 2027.

The raise would fund AI and data-center buildout tied to Elon Musk's wider ambitions. Reuters notes SpaceX has become an increasingly large buyer of AI hardware as it expands compute for internal workloads and its satellite/data businesses.

The structure matters more than the headline number. Rather than paying for chips from operating cash, the company is borrowing against future capacity — the same pattern now spreading across the sector. Financial Express framed the SpaceX package as a bellwether test for AI-linked debt markets, asking whether investors will keep absorbing this scale of borrowing.
sections.whyItMatters: Frontier AI hardware is increasingly financed like infrastructure — via structured debt and special-purpose vehicles — which ties the sector's growth to credit-market appetite, not just chip supply.

sections.heading: Broadcom in Talks for $60 Billion-Plus to Fund Anthropic's Chips
sections.body:
Broadcom is negotiating more than $60 billion in debt to finance AI chips for Anthropic and other customers, with total figures under discussion potentially reaching $100 billion, Bloomberg reported via TNW. Blackstone and Apollo are reportedly in talks to participate.

The package is described as having two parts: a junior tranche of roughly $30 billion alongside a $60-70 billion senior-secured tranche, issued through a special-purpose vehicle. Broadcom would guarantee part of the senior tranche, which Bloomberg says has allowed senior notes to obtain investment-grade ratings and lower borrowing costs. Under the arrangement, Anthropic does not buy the chips directly — investors finance the purchase and lease the hardware to the company.

The financing extends a partnership — Broadcom, Apollo and Blackstone's AI XPV — whose opening transaction raised $35 billion to expand Anthropic's compute. The partners aim to finance more than 20 gigawatts of computing power by 2028; the first $35 billion commitment covers about one gigawatt, roughly a twentieth of the stated target.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the clearest example yet of vendors and Wall Street splitting the risk of AI buildout: Broadcom backstops debt, private-credit firms hold the asset, and the AI lab rents capacity instead of owning it.

sections.heading: US Charges California CEO in $300M Nvidia Server Smuggling Case
sections.body:
The US arrested Greg Lui, owner of City of Industry, California-based Earthmade Computer Inc., on federal charges that he arranged the illegal export of more than $300 million in export-controlled technology to China, including advanced Nvidia-equipped servers, according to DOJ reporting cited by Export Compliance Daily and Ars Technica.

Prosecutors allege shipments were routed through Singapore and Malaysia and onward to Hong Kong before reaching a Chinese firm based in Hangzhou. The indictment reportedly cites $176 million linked to Malaysia alone, and describes the use of false records and overseas intermediaries to disguise the end destination.

The case lands as Washington debates the effectiveness of its chip controls. Goldman Sachs has published a 10-year projection suggesting China could still be roughly 34% short of advanced-node chip self-sufficiency in 2035, with SMIC's yields flagged as a fragile variable — a reminder that enforcement and domestic-capacity questions are two halves of the same policy problem.
sections.whyItMatters: The scale of the alleged scheme — a single California firm allegedly moving a third of a billion dollars in restricted hardware — underscores how much of the export-control regime now depends on enforcement against intermediaries, not just formal licensing.

sections.heading: Minnesota Water Systems Hit as Attribution Stays Contested
sections.body:
Federal investigators are probing what state officials describe as a coordinated cyberattack on more than 30 community water systems across Minnesota, which disrupted operations and forced several utilities to switch to manual controls, according to WION and state reporting. Four cities have publicly confirmed the incidents.

Investigators are examining whether the hackers have links to Iranian cyber groups, but the FBI has cautioned that findings remain preliminary. Officials are also weighing whether the attackers intentionally tried to appear Iran-based amid heightened US-Iran tensions. Iran separately said it thwarted an 'extensive, complex' cyberattack on its own communications infrastructure, according to Anadolu Agency — a claim that adds to a two-way pattern of contested attribution.

The incident reinforces a recurring gap: small and mid-sized US utilities operate aging operational-technology systems that are hard to patch and slow to staff.
sections.whyItMatters: Attribution in the water-sector incidents is deliberately murky — the FBI is not yet confirming an Iran link — which shows how low-cost false flags and borrowed toolkits complicate deterrence even when the target set is well known.

sections.heading: Europe's Huawei Fight Shifts to Cost and Timetables
sections.body:
Seventeen CEOs from major European operators — including Orange, Deutsche Telekom and Telefónica — have signed an open letter urging the EU to reconsider plans to force out 'high-risk' network suppliers, warning the move could cost the sector up to €40 billion, per GSMA estimates reported by euronews and MSN.

The pressure is producing movement. EU governments have reportedly dropped a proposed three-year deadline for removing high-risk equipment from mobile networks, per a proposal seen by Reuters, and operators may get more time to phase out incumbent gear. Vodafone has nonetheless begun preparing for Huawei removal irrespective of the Brussels timeline.

In Portugal, Altice's Meo has launched an €82 million legal action against the state over its Huawei 5G exclusion, arguing its deployment was disrupted by the ban — a sign that national decisions are now generating their own litigation.
sections.whyItMatters: The debate has moved from security principle to who pays: the €40 billion figure and the dropped deadline show cost calculations now shape the pace of European vendor removal.

sections.heading: Space Race Narrows: Türkiye's Aselsan Unveils Satellite Constellation as Europe Launches ISR Bird
sections.body:
Türkiye's Aselsan unveiled Gokbagi, a homegrown low-Earth-orbit communications satellite constellation, at the International Astronautical Congress, with first launches expected within a few years, according to Türkiye Today, Yeni Safak and Anadolu Agency. Anadolu reported the network is described as dual-use, intended to provide rapid, secure communications for Turkish military and public users.

In Europe, Rheinmetall's Italian subsidiary and Argotec launched their first satellite — carried to orbit on a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Vandenberg Space Force Base — to provide space-based data for military air defense and early warning, per The Defense Post and Rheinmetall. The two firms are building toward an independent space-based surveillance capability.

South Korea's homegrown Nuri rocket launched 15 satellites from the Naro Space Center, including five ultra-small cluster satellites placed at roughly 570 kilometers and ten cube satellites — the country's first domestic deployment of a satellite constellation, per the Korea Herald and UPI.
sections.whyItMatters: Middle and smaller powers are moving from buying space services to fielding their own constellations, eroding the assumption that military communications and ISR depend on a handful of major providers.

sections.heading: Rare-Earth Clock: China's Nov. 10 Deadline Nears as Congress Moves
sections.body:
Two converging deadlines are shaping the critical-minerals standoff: the reported expiry of China's rare-earth export suspension on November 10, 2026, and the full effect of the DFARS defense procurement ban on January 1, 2027, per MSN reporting. China has said it will 'optimize' its latest export controls while insisting they are not aimed at any third party, according to Xinhua via Anadolu Agency.

Congress is advancing legislation to reduce dependency, including measures on mine permits, a $2.5 billion reserve and defense supply-chain provisions — bills that must still clear the Senate. Underlying the exposure: IEA figures cited by Seeking Alpha put China at roughly 60% of mined magnet rare earths and 91% of refined output.
sections.whyItMatters: The November deadline is a hard test of whether Western diversification efforts have built enough slack to absorb a renewed export squeeze — current refining concentration suggests they have not.

bottomLine: Today's defining development was financial rather than technical: SpaceX's $40 billion chip-financing effort and Broadcom's $60 billion-plus Anthropic package show that frontier AI compute is being bought with structured debt and leased back to the labs that use it. That spreads the risk of the AI buildout across private-credit markets, tying its pace to investor appetite as much as to fab capacity or export rules. Elsewhere, the Nvidia smuggling indictment, the murky Minnesota water-sector hack and Europe's cost-driven Huawei retreat all point to the same reality: enforcement, attribution and vendor removal are slower and messier than the policies that mandate them.
sources: Reuters, Financial Times (via Reuters), Bloomberg (via TNW), TNW, Financial Express, Export Compliance Daily, Ars Technica, WION, Anadolu Agency, euronews, GSMA, Reuters (EU proposal), TelecomTV, Türkiye Today, Yeni Safak, The Defense Post, Rheinmetall, Korea Herald, UPI, MSN, Xinhua, Seeking Alpha (IEA data), Goldman Sachs (via TechTimes), Cryptobriefing
